name: Opus Value
strategy: Contrarian value in capitulated quality, concentrated in the managed-care margin-recovery trade and cheap cash-flow IT, with the mandated inflation-shock hedge upgraded from staples-and-crypto to integrated energy plus physical gold now that an oil-driven stagflation is the confirmed regime.
reassessment_note: Three things changed. (1) The inflation shock my mandate told me to hedge has actually arrived and it is an energy shock: WTI $91 and Brent $100, both roughly +50% year-over-year, with core PCE marked up to 3.4% and the Fed hiking to 3.75-4.00% in September for the first time since 2023. (2) It now comes with a growth crack: September payrolls were 29K against 84K expected, July revised to -10K, unemployment 4.2%. That combination is stagflation, and in stagflation a 20% cash buffer earning 4% against 3%+ inflation is not safety, it is a slow loss. I cut cash to 15% and moved the proceeds into real assets. (3) Two legs were contradicting my own strategy of record. PEP was a bond-proxy staple I had already said I was moving away from, and it is now down ~10% YTD, ~24% from its high, with JPMorgan cutting to Neutral and Frito-Lay's recovery stalled -- cheap, but broken, and a value trap rather than a mean-reversion candidate. QCOM's cheapness no longer holds either: consensus is Hold, the mean target of ~$191 is essentially where it trades, and the Apple content loss is structural, not cyclical. Both are gone. In their place I added physical gold, which is the asset actually responding to this regime (bullion ~$4,170 after a $4,690 futures peak, an ~11% pullback inside an intact uptrend -- a contrarian entry into a confirmed hedge), and I concentrated harder into the one cluster where cheapness, quality, a live catalyst and defensiveness all coincide: managed care at 30% of the book. I deliberately did NOT buy gold miners here for this book; GDX is at decade highs and is a momentum instrument, not a value one, so the value book takes the metal and leaves the equity beta alone.

positions.thesis: My largest position and the core of the book. The margin-recovery thesis is no longer a hope: FY26 adjusted EPS guidance was raised to $19.50-$20.00 and management is deliberately shedding 1.3-1.4m Medicare Advantage lives to buy back margin rather than defend volume, which is exactly the capital discipline a contrarian wants to see from a capitulated compounder. The stock is up ~40% from its March lows and still sits at $371.90 against a $480 mean target with 19 of 26 analysts at Strong Buy, so the re-rating is only partly done. It is also the right thing to own into a weakening labour market: healthcare utilisation is non-discretionary and the revenue is not consumer-cyclical. Upsized from 14% because this is my highest-conviction idea and the brief imposes no position cap.

The cheapest high-quality name I could find anywhere in this market: a 9.6x forward P/E, roughly half the sector average, on $30.50 of 2026 consensus EPS. It rides the same moderating-medical-cost-trend tailwind that is re-rating the whole MCO group (covered managed-care shares up ~35% on average since September 2025) but has participated far less, which is the definition of the mean-reversion setup this book exists to own. Pairing it with UNH makes managed care 30% of the book -- intentional concentration into one thesis expressed through the premium operator and the deep-value operator, so I am paid whether the group re-rates on earnings delivery or on multiple catch-up.

The primary expression of the mandated inflation-shock hedge, and it is now hedging a shock that is actually happening rather than a hypothetical one. Brent at ~$100 and WTI at ~$91, both up about 50% year-over-year, is the proximate cause of the 3.4% core PCE that forced the Fed's hand, so this leg is long the thing that is driving the macro pain in every other asset I own. Integrated energy is still priced well below what $90+ crude implies for mid-cycle free cash flow, which keeps it inside a value mandate rather than being a momentum chase. Added a point and left the take-profit off deliberately: a hedge against an open-ended inflation shock should not be capped, and capping it last quarter is the kind of thing that makes a hedge stop working exactly when you need it.

Working as intended at +6.87% and retained near full size. Cheap IT services is the right kind of cash-flow value for a stagflation: the revenue is contracted and recurring, the business is asset-light so there is little input-cost exposure to $91 oil, and corporate AI implementation spend is a genuine demand tailwind rather than a cost line. Trimmed a point only to fund the gold hedge, not because the thesis weakened.

New leg, and the single most important change in this book. My mandate requires an inflation-shock hedge, and gold is the asset that is actually responding to this one: bullion ran from below $4,000 in late June to above $4,600 in August and sits ~$4,170 now, an ~11% pullback inside an unbroken uptrend, which is a contrarian entry rather than a breakout chase. It hedges the specific thing cash cannot: a Fed that is hiking into 3.4% core inflation and has just been handed a 29K payroll print, which is the setup where real yields fall, policy credibility is questioned, and the metal re-rates. I chose the bullion trust over the miners on purpose -- GDX is at decade highs and up 53% year-over-year, so miners are a momentum instrument whose cheapness has already been arbitraged away, while GLD gives me the hedge with no operating leverage, no single-asset risk and no equity beta bleeding into a book that is already 30% long one equity theme.

The second leg of the energy hedge, held alongside XOM to spread single-name operational risk across two integrateds rather than concentrating the mandate's hedge in one balance sheet. Up 1.48% since entry, with a dividend and buyback profile that is comfortably covered at $90 crude. Added a point as part of shifting cash into real assets; no take-profit, for the same reason as XOM.

The purest capitulated-quality setup left in the book, so I added to it on weakness instead of cutting the loser. Q3 was a beat on both lines -- $6.13 EPS against $6.08, revenue $6.76bn up 12.9% -- and management raised full-year guidance to $26.58-26.63bn revenue and $24.45-24.50 EPS, yet the stock is down 4.74% on my leg. The market is paying for the generative-AI competitive narrative and refusing to pay for accelerating reported results, which is exactly the gap mean-reversion harvests. I keep it small and give it a wide 18% stop because the bear case, that AI genuinely compresses creative-software pricing, is a real structural risk and not one I can disprove.

Trimmed from 4% to 3% and kept only as a token hard-asset leg. The honest assessment is that it has not done its job: BTC is up 32% over this book's life while ETH has gone sideways and is down 3.90% on my leg, so as a debasement hedge it has been dominated by both bitcoin and gold. It has at least just broken out of the $2,600 range it held since September 24 to ~$2,757 on short liquidations and easing front-end yields, so I am not selling into the one piece of good news it has had. But the capital it was really holding belongs in GLD, which is why the gold leg is 11% and this one is 3%. The 35bps round-trip on crypto is also a reason to shrink rather than churn it.
